scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Waacking originated in Los Angeles during the early 1970s inside LGBTQ+ nightclubs, created primarily by African American and Latino dancers.
It began as punking, a name derived from a derogatory slur aimed at gay men, which performers inverted into an expressive, narrative dance style.
Dancers moved to underground and imported disco music that DJs sped up to produce an intense, energetic atmosphere.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: In its original gay club context, punking and waacking served as an outlet of creative liberation, sensual expression, and self-definition for marginalized queer, Black, and Latino dancers facing social hostility.
The dance provided a theatrical space to emulate glamorous Hollywood divas and enact personal stories through heightened physicality.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The style is executed through rapid, rotational arm sweeps, explosive rhythmic strikes, and theatrical poses coordinated with music.
Dancers whip their forearms and wrists around and behind the head and across the shoulder line, isolating sharp gestures while maintaining rhythmic syncopation.
A key technical element is posing, in which dancers freeze into glamorous, heightened diva stances inspired by Hollywood movie figures.
Watch for The Whack, Posing, Rotational Arm Rolls.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Waacking was founded on 1970s disco and funk, specifically underground and imported disco records that were often sped up on club turntables to increase dance floor energy.
Over subsequent decades, the dance adapted to 1980s post-disco, electro sounds, and modern music varieties, though disco remains its historical and primary sonic foundation.
Listen for the Drum kit, Electric bass, Rhythm guitar, String section.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 127 beats a minute.

High-octane 1970s disco and post-disco characterized by a relentless four-on-the-floor beat, syncopated basslines, and soaring orchestral strings. The music delivers dramatic brass accents and vocal peaks that cue sharp, sudden arm hits and frozen poses.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical and contemporary figures include Jeffrey Daniel, who added the 'g' to the name; Tyrone Proctor (1953–2020), a pioneering Los Angeles creator and Soul Train dancer; Brian 'Footwork' Green, who initiated the 2003 global revival through workshops; Kumari Suraj, who choreographed a milestone 2011 routine on So You Think You Can Dance; and French waacker Josépha Madoki, who danced in the 2018 'Apeshit' music video by Beyoncé and Jay-Z. Other notable practitioners named in sources include Bruno Marignan, Sandrine Sainte Croix, Lil Kiss, Princess Lockeroo, Mariana Benenge, Mounia Nassangar, Habibitch, Boubou, choreographer Axelle Munezero, and Olympic champions Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron.
Waacking originated in Los Angeles, California, developing alongside New York City's parallel ballroom voguing culture on the East Coast of the United States.
Waacking evolved directly out of punking in 1970s Los Angeles gay clubs, absorbing stylistic and physical principles from jazz dance, gymnastics, martial arts, and Hollywood screen performance.

visual_brief.setting_notes: In its original gay club context, punking and waacking served as an outlet of creative liberation, sensual expression, and self-definition for marginalized queer, Black, and Latino dancers facing social hostility.
